title: Chu Berry picks up the tenor at the Colonnades
summary: At the Colonnades with Fat Man Turner's Arcadians, Chu Berry filled in on tenor when the tenor player did not show and kept it.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well now, we're getting to the end of this. I don't have any sort of memories of yours, particularly memories of yours, you know, of big musical occasions or anything you'd like to -- or funny events, anything you'd like to record.
(Recording interruption)
When you first heard him?
Chu was playing alto. Chu was working down at the Colonnades when I was down there with -- with Arthur Gibbs, and Fat Man Turner, the bass player, had taken the band into the Colonnades.
Well, he had a band called the Arcadians

Right. That's true. And I forgot who the tenor player was. Anyway, Chu was on alto. That's one of those things that happened, a coincidence, and the tenor player didn't show. So they requested -- we always used three saxophones, alto, two altos and a tenor. So the tenor man didn't show, so they had to substitute another alto. So Chu picked up the tenor because we leave the tenors -- at that time in those barrooms -- unprotected. You could leave them on the stand, right on the stand. When it comes to the break, you leave them on the stand right in there.
Really?
That's right.
Well, why was that? I mean --
They have a lot of guys didn't worry about taking them home or --
I mean was there better protection or something?
Sure, because they had guards. They
had guards there and a couple of guys there all night.
So Chu just picked up this --
We picked up the horn -- I'd just leave mine there too. And (unintelligible) it up, fill in, tenor player wasn't there that night. Chu Then Chu liked it. Chu stayed on it. That was it.
Well, in a way you might almost say, when you point that out, that you can partly hear that.
That's true.
You know? I mean that is -- there's something a little of the alto in that.
It is. Yeah, this is quite true.

But he was -- I mean he's another guy that is, you know, as the history of jazz lengthens, people like that get forgotten. You know, they say Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster, Lester Young, and then you -- you know, there's -- but I mean he was a great guy. I mean --
Yes, he was.
I mean that was a very distinctive style and --
Very.
He certainly was one of the swingingest ever.
That's right, he sure was.
Yeah.
